claim: A cell-site simulator — commercially a "Stingray," generically an IMSI catcher — mimics a cell tower so that every phone nearby connects to it and hands over its identity and location, whether or not it belongs to a suspect. US police acquired them under a secrecy regime run by the FBI: before a department could buy a Stingray from its maker, the Harris Corporation, "the FBI requires the local agency to sign a lengthy nondisclosure agreement." The ACLU and journalists pried the agreements loose through public-records requests. The NDAs "forced [agencies to] hide it from judges and defense attorneys in court proceedings," and some agencies went "as far as dismissing criminal prosecutions instead of revealing accurate information about tech surveillance to criminal defense lawyers."

sources.label: ACLU — "Documents in ACLU Case Reveal More Detail on FBI Attempt to Cover Up Stingray Technology." The Harris Corporation / FBI nondisclosure-agreement requirement.
sources.quote: the FBI requires the local agency to sign a lengthy nondisclosure agreement before buying the device.
